doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Father's role in New Orleans big band and school music education
summary: His father taught at Booker T. Washington in 1947, disguised Ellington as symphonic arrangements, and helped found music education in Orleans Parish.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Your father was credited somewhere they called him “the father of New Orleans big band?”

Yeah you can use some of that terminology. Yeah I would give him credit for doing that. Actually he was one of the people who started music education in the schools. Not only big band but he was one of the founders of — there was a book called Changes on the Chalkboard by Al Kennedy. Changes on the Chalkboard I think it’s Shawnee Press if you ever need a good book, and it deals with music education in the Orleans Parish school system. And my father was one of those who was very instrumental in getting it together. Now he graduated from Xavier University with a degree in English and science and that’s what he was teaching in the beginning of his career. But he wound up teaching music for most of all his life in the school system. But his approach to music was from the same type of mindset of science teaching you might say. He taught at a school in New Orleans, Booker T. Washington, in 1947. The principal at the school didn’t like jazz so he didn’t want a band. But he was teaching English and science but he also had the band. So what he would do, man, he would take a Duke Ellington tune and put it in a symphonic type of form and arrangement so he was able to play that and this guy didn’t even know the difference man. You know how it was back when jazz was a bad word, you know, the Devil’s music and all that kind of stuff you know.
I’ll be darned, even in New Orleans, huh?
